The Prophet told an Ansari woman who missed Hajj, having only two water camels, to perform Umrah in Ramadan, for it equals Hajj.
The Prophet entered Mecca from its upper side and left by the lower, after a night at Dhi Tuwa praying dawn on a hillock; he left Medina by al-Shajara.
The Prophet had three circuits walked swiftly and four normally so polytheists who thought fever had weakened the Muslims saw their strength; he rode between Safa and Marwa amid crowds.
The Prophet touched only the Black Stone and Yamani corners; Umar kissed the Stone, saying he knew it was a stone but had seen the Prophet kiss it.
At the Farewell Pilgrimage the Prophet circled the Ka'ba riding, touching the Corner with a stick so people could see and question him; ailing Umm Salama rode behind the people.
Aisha explains the verse calling Safa and Marwa Allah's signs: the Ansar, who once said Talbiya for idols, shunned going between them; Sa'i is the Prophet's Sunnah, done once.
The Prophet kept up Talbiya from Arafat until stoning Jamrat al-Aqaba, Ibn Mas'ud said it at Muzdalifa, and going from Mina to Arafat some said Talbiya, Takbir or Tahlil unopposed.
Riding from Arafat at a measured pace, the Prophet stopped in a valley for light ablution, telling Usama the prayer lay ahead, and prayed sunset and Isha at Muzdalifa.
At Muzdalifa the Prophet combined sunset and Isha with one iqama, three and two rak'ahs and nothing between; only these and that day's early dawn prayer left their usual times.
The Prophet let Sauda, Umm Habiba, women and the weak leave Muzdalifa by night before the crowd, as Aisha wished she had, and Asma and Ibn Umar's household stoned early.
Ibn Mas'ud threw seven pebbles at Jamrat al-Aqaba from the valley's heart, as the Prophet had; the Prophet stoned riding, telling people to learn the rites, and enjoined odd numbers.
The Prophet prayed repeatedly for those who shaved, then for those who clipped; after stoning and sacrificing he was shaved, right side first, the hair given out to people.
At Mina in the Farewell Pilgrimage, asked about shaving before sacrificing or sacrificing before stoning, the Prophet answered every question of order: do it, there is no harm.
Asked on the Day of Nahr about stoning, sacrificing, shaving or Tawaf al-Ifada done out of order, the Prophet saw no harm; he prayed noon at Mina after the Tawaf.
The Prophet prayed noon at Mina on Tarwiya and later halted at al-Abtah (Muhassab), where Quraysh pledged against Banu Hashim; Aisha says it is no Sunnah, just easy for departing.
Al-Abbas was allowed to spend Mina's nights in Mecca to water the pilgrims, and Ibn Abbas's family serves nabidh because the Prophet drank it there and approved.
The Prophet put Ali in charge of his sacrificial animals, to give all their meat, skins and saddle cloths to the poor and nothing to the butcher as wages.
At Hudaibiya and in Hajj seven people shared one camel or cow; the Prophet sacrificed for his wives, a cow for Aisha; a camel is slaughtered standing, fettered.
Aisha wove garlands for the sacrificial animals, goats included, that the Prophet sent to Mecca while he stayed in Medina avoiding nothing a Muhrim avoids, contrary to Ibn Abbas's view.
The Prophet told a man driving a sacrificial camel to ride it, gently until another mount is found; exhausted ones are slaughtered, marked with blood, not eaten by their escort.
Pilgrims must make circling the House their last act before leaving, but menstruating women are excused, so Safiyyah, menstruating after Tawaf al-Ifada, was allowed to set off.
In the year of Victory the Prophet entered the Ka'bah with Usama, Bilal and Uthman b. Talha and prayed between its pillars; Usama said he only supplicated inside.
But for his people's recent unbelief the Prophet would have rebuilt the Ka'bah on Abraham's foundations with the Hijr; Ibn Zubair did, and Abd al-Malik undid the Hijr part.
A Khath'am woman may perform Hajj for her aged father who cannot ride, and a child lifted up to the Prophet is credited with Hajj, with reward for his mother.
Told that Hajj is obligatory, a man asked if it is every year; the Prophet said a yes would bind them, and warned that excessive questioning destroyed earlier peoples.
A woman believing in Allah and the Last Day may not travel a day, a night, two days or three without her husband, father, son, brother or another Mahram.
No man may be alone with a woman without a Mahram, nor a woman travel without one; a man enlisted for battle is told to join his wife's Hajj.
Setting out, the Prophet said Takbir thrice and asked Allah for piety, ease and protection; returning from battle, Hajj or Umrah he said Takbir on high ground, praising his Lord.
The Prophet halted and prayed at the stony ground of Dhu'l-Hulaifa, where he was told at night it is blessed, and Ibn Umar halted there returning from Hajj or Umrah.
Abu Bakr, leading the Hajj before the Farewell Pilgrimage, sent criers on the Day of Nahr: after that year no polytheist may make Hajj nor naked person circle the House.
Allah frees more servants from Hell on the Day of Arafa than any other; Umrah expiates sins until the next; accepted Hajj earns Paradise; pilgrims without indecency return sinless.
Asked where he would stay in Mecca, the Prophet asked whether Aqil had left any house, as Aqil and Talib, not the Muslims Ja'far and Ali, had inherited Abu Talib.
An emigrant may stay in Mecca only three days after completing the rites of Hajj.
At the Conquest the Prophet said Allah made Mecca sacred at creation, fighting there allowed him one hour only; its thorns, game, herbage and lost things are protected, weapons forbidden.
The Prophet entered Mecca in the Year of Victory in a helmet, or a black turban without Ihram, and ordered Ibn Khatal killed though he clung to the Ka'bah's curtains.
As Abraham made Mecca sacred, the Prophet made Medina sacred between its lava plains, protecting its trees and game, and prayed for blessing in its measures; innovators there are cursed.
Ali quotes the Prophet: Medina is sacred from Air to Thaur, cursing innovators, breakers of a Muslim's protection and false claimants of lineage; Abu Huraira would not disturb its deer.
The Prophet prayed over first fruits for blessing on Medina double Mecca's and made it sacred, its passes guarded by angels; Abu Sa'id urged staying there despite hardship.
The Prophet asked Allah to make unhealthy Medina as congenial as Mecca and move its fever to al-Juhfa, and will be intercessor or witness for whoever endures its hardships.
Angels guard Medina from plague and the Dajjal; like a furnace it drives out its impurities, and its name is Medina, or Taba, not Yathrib.
Allah dissolves like salt whoever means harm to Medina's people; some will leave for conquered Syria, Yemen and Iraq though it is better, and it will be left to beasts.
Between the Prophet's house and pulpit is a garden of Paradise, his pulpit stands on his cistern, and Uhud is a mountain that loves them and that they love.
Prayer in the Prophet's mosque is better than a thousand elsewhere except the Sacred Mosque; Maimuna told a woman who vowed to pray in Bait al-Maqdis to pray there instead.
Journeys are undertaken only to three mosques, the Sacred Mosque, the Prophet's and al-Aqsa, and the mosque founded on piety is the Prophet's mosque in Medina.
The Prophet came to Quba, riding or on foot, every Saturday and prayed two rak'ahs in its mosque, and Ibn Umar did the same.
The Prophet told young men who can support a wife to marry, or else fast, and rejected companions' vows of celibacy, Uthman b. Maz'un's included, saying he himself marries.
After seeing a woman the Prophet went to his wife Zainab, and said whoever is captivated by a woman should go to his own wife, which repels what he feels.
Castration was forbidden and temporary marriage permitted; Jabir says it was practised until Umar forbade it, and another report says it was allowed three nights at Autas, then forbidden.
Sabra contracted a temporary marriage for his cloak in the Year of Victory, then the Prophet forbade it until the Day of Resurrection; Ibn Zubair and Ibn Abbas disputed it.
Ali told Ibn Abbas that on the Day of Khaibar the Prophet forbade temporary marriage forever, along with the flesh of domestic asses.
A woman may not be married together with her paternal or maternal aunt, nor seek her sister's divorce to take her share, nor a man propose over his brother's proposal.
A Muhrim may neither marry, arrange a marriage nor propose, Uthman reports; Ibn Abbas says the Prophet married Maimuna in Ihram, while Maimuna says he was not.
None may propose over his brother's proposal or bargain over his bargain until he gives way, nor a townsman sell for a villager, nor a woman seek her sister's divorce.
The Prophet forbade Shighar, exchanging daughters or sisters in marriage with no dower, and said the conditions most worthy of fulfilment are those that make intercourse lawful.
A previously married woman must be consulted and has more right to herself than her guardian; a virgin's permission is asked, her silence being her consent.
Aisha says the Prophet married her at six, or seven, and took her to his house at nine with her dolls, both in Shawwal; she was eighteen when he died.
The Prophet told a man marrying an Ansari woman to look at her, and found his dower of four uqiyas too much, sending him on an expedition.
A man without even an iron ring is married for the Quran he knows; the Prophet's dower was five hundred dirhams; Abd al-Rahman married for a date-stone of gold.
At Khaibar the Prophet took the captive Safiyya from Dihya, made her freedom her dower, held a hais wedding feast and veiled her; freeing then marrying earns two rewards.
Guests lingered talking after the Prophet's wedding feast for Zainab, his most lavish, until he hung a curtain and the verse on entering his houses only when invited came down.
One invited to a wedding feast or other feast should accept, even for a sheep's leg, and may eat or not; one who is fasting should pray for the hosts.
The worst food is a wedding feast where the rich are invited and the poor turned away, yet whoever refuses an invitation disobeys Allah and His Messenger.
A woman divorced by three pronouncements cannot return to her first husband until her second husband has consummated the marriage, as the Prophet told Rifa'a's former wife.
Saying Allah's name before going to one's wife keeps Satan from the child; the tilth verse answered a Jewish claim, allowing intercourse from behind or in front through one opening.
Angels curse a wife who refuses her husband's bed until morning, and the worst man before Allah on Judgement Day is one who divulges his wife's intimate secrets.
On the Banu al-Mustaliq expedition men asked about 'azl with captive women; the Prophet said every soul destined to be born until the Day of Resurrection will be born.
Asked about 'azl, the Prophet said there is no harm in not practising it, since a child Allah has ordained will come, and nothing prevents what He intends to create.
Told what was decreed would come, a man practising 'azl with his slave-girl found her pregnant; Jabir said they practised it in the Prophet's lifetime without his forbidding it.
The Prophet meant to curse one approaching a pregnant woman whose child he could not lawfully own, did not forbid relations with nursing women, and called 'azl secret burying alive.
Fosterage forbids what blood kinship forbids, so Aisha was told to admit Aflah, brother of her foster-father Abu'l-Qu'ais, as her uncle, though a woman, not a man, had suckled her.
Hamza's daughter was unlawful to the Prophet as his foster-brother's daughter, as was Durrah bint Abu Salama, for Thuwaiba suckled him and Abu Salama; Umm Habiba's sister was unlawful too.
One or two sucklings do not make marriage unlawful; Aisha said the Quran had revealed ten clear sucklings as making it unlawful, later replaced by five.
Sahla was told to suckle the grown Salim so he could enter freely, easing Abu Hudhaifa's displeasure; the Prophet's other wives, unlike Aisha, held it a concession for Salim alone.
Displeased to find a man with Aisha, who said he was her foster-brother, the Prophet told her to consider who her foster-brothers are, for fosterage is through hunger.
After captives were taken at Autas during Hunain, the Companions refrained from intercourse with captive women with polytheist husbands until a verse made those their right hands possess lawful.
The child belongs to the bed, and stoning is for the fornicator, the Prophet ruled over a disputed boy; he rejoiced when a physiognomist found Zaid's and Usama's feet related.
Marrying Umm Salama, the Prophet stayed three nights, offering a week only if every wife got one; a new virgin bride is given seven nights, a previously married one three.
The Prophet divided nights among nine wives; Abu Bakr rebuked Aisha for quarrelling with Zainab, Sauda gave Aisha her day, and Aisha remarked on the verse letting him defer wives.
A woman is married for property, status, beauty or religion, so choose religion; asked why not a virgin, Jabir said his previously married wife could care for his sisters.
A pious woman is the world's best provision; woman, created from a rib, breaks if straightened, so treat women kindly; without Eve no woman would be unfaithful to her husband.
Ibn Umar, who divorced his wife while menstruating, was told to take her back and divorce her, if at all, when pure, before touching her, as Allah commanded.
Ibn Umar told questioners his one divorce pronounced during menstruation was counted, though he took her back; the Prophet recited the verse on divorcing women at their prescribed period.
Ibn Abbas said three pronouncements of divorce counted as one under the Prophet, Abu Bakr and early in Umar's caliphate, until Umar, as people hastened to divorce, imposed them.
Ibn Abbas said a man declaring his wife unlawful to himself has sworn an oath that must be expiated, citing the Messenger of Allah as the model.
Aisha and other wives agreed to say the Prophet smelled of maghafir after he drank honey at Zainab's or Hafsa's, so he gave it up, and verses came down.
Commanded to give his wives a choice, the Prophet began with Aisha, who chose Allah, His Messenger and the Hereafter, as all did, and he sought their leave on turns.
Aisha said when the Prophet gave his wives the option and they chose him, he did not count it as divorce, nor did Masruq mind giving his wife the option.
Pressed by his wives for money, the Prophet kept away from them twenty-nine days in his attic, where Umar found him on a mat, until the verse of choice came.
Fatima bint Qais, irrevocably divorced, was told she had no maintenance or lodging, to spend her waiting period at blind Ibn Umm Maktum's and to marry Usama; Marwan rejected it.
Al-Aswad cited Umar rejecting a woman's word on lodging against Allah's Book; Fatima told how the Prophet called Mu'awiya poor and Abu Jahm harsh with women, urging Usama instead.
Aisha faulted a divorced woman for leaving her husband's house and said no good came of Fatima citing her case; Jabir's divorced aunt was allowed out to pluck dates.
The Prophet told Subai'a, widowed while pregnant, she could marry after giving birth, as Umm Salama confirmed when Ibn Abbas and Abu Salama disputed such a widow's waiting period.
A believing woman mourns no one beyond three days except her husband, four months and ten days, which the Prophet contrasted with a pre-Islamic year when refusing a widow collyrium.
A woman mourns no one beyond three days except her husband, four months and ten days, without collyrium, perfume or dyed garments, save a little incense after her courses.
Uwaimir asked about a man finding another with his wife; under the revealed verses spouses swore four oaths and a fifth curse, were separated, and the dower stayed hers.
After mutual cursing, children were born as the Prophet foretold or resembling the accused man; Ibn Abbas said the Prophet's words on stoning without evidence concerned another woman.
Sa'd b. Ubada, ready to kill a man found with his wife, was told to bring four witnesses; the Prophet called himself more jealous than Sa'd, and Allah more so.
A dark child, like a dusky camel among red ones, may reflect a reverted strain, the Prophet told a man wanting to disown his son, and did not permit it.
A co-owner freeing his share frees the slave fully if he can pay partners a fair price; otherwise the slave is partly freed or works, not overburdened, for the rest.
Barira's owners would sell her only keeping her wala; the Prophet said wala is the freer's and conditions outside Allah's Book are void; freed, she chose to leave her husband.
Selling or gifting the wala is forbidden, and whoever takes a freed slave as ally without his former master's consent bears the curse of Allah, the angels and all mankind.
Whoever frees a Muslim slave, Allah frees from the Fire a limb of his for every limb of the slave; on hearing this Ali b. Husain freed a costly slave.
A son cannot repay what he owes his father unless he finds him a slave, buys him and sets him free.
The Prophet forbade the sales called mulamasa and munabadha, closing a deal by touching or throwing a garment without inspecting it, and also two ways of dressing.
The Prophet forbade sales settled by throwing a pebble, sales involving uncertainty, and habal al-habala, a sale deferred until a she-camel's offspring is born and itself becomes pregnant.
A Muslim must not enter a sale while his brother is bargaining, nor propose marriage over his brother's proposal unless he permits it.
The Prophet forbade meeting caravans on the way, outbidding, buying against a brother, a townsman selling for a desert dweller, tying animals' udders, and a woman seeking her sister's divorce.
Merchandise and traders must not be met on the way before they reach the market; a seller bought from that way may cancel the sale on reaching it.
A townsman must not sell on behalf of a man from the desert, even his brother or father; Ibn Abbas explained it as acting as his broker.
Whoever buys a goat or she-camel whose udder was tied up may keep it after milking, or return it within three days with a sa' of dates, not wheat.
Whoever buys foodgrain must not resell it before taking possession and measuring it; people were beaten for reselling on the spot, and Marwan stopped sales made by documents.
The Prophet forbade selling a heap of dates of unknown weight for a known measure of dates.
Both parties to a sale may annul it until they separate, unless an option was agreed; honest, open dealing is blessed, while lying and concealment wipe out the blessing.
A man who was cheated in sales was told by the Prophet to say, when making a deal, that there should be no deception.
The Prophet forbade seller and buyer to trade fruit before its good condition is clear, when it turns red or yellow, is fit to eat and safe from blight.
While forbidding fresh dates on the tree for dry dates, the Prophet allowed the 'ariyya, by which a household gives measured dry dates for fresh dates to eat.
Selling fresh dates for dry dates is riba and muzabana, except for families given a tree or two as 'ariyya, allowed for up to five wasqs or less.
The Prophet forbade muzabana: selling fresh dates on the tree for dry dates, grapes for raisins, or standing crops for grain, by measure or by estimate.
When pollinated palms are sold their fruit belongs to the seller, and when a slave is sold his property belongs to the seller, unless the buyer stipulates otherwise.
The Prophet forbade muhaqala, muzabana, mukhabara, sales years ahead and fruit before it ripens, and sales except for dinars and dirhams, 'araya excepted; Jabir explained the terms.
The Prophet forbade renting out land or taking a share of its crop: an owner should cultivate it himself, lend it free to his brother, or keep it.
The Prophet forbade renting land or selling its produce years ahead, and muzabana and muhaqala, the latter explained as renting land; an owner should cultivate or lend it.
Ibn Umar rented out his land until Rafi b. Khadij told him, from his uncles, that the Prophet had forbidden renting land, and then he gave it up.
Rafi b. Khadij's uncle conveyed the Prophet's ban on renting land for a third or quarter of its crop or measured grain: cultivate it, have it cultivated, or keep it.
Renting land for gold or silver is allowed; what was forbidden was letting land for the crop of one plot, which might fail, and sharecropping, rent being permitted.
Ibn Abbas held that the Prophet did not forbid renting land outright, but said lending it to one's brother is better than taking a fixed return from it.
The Prophet let Khaibar's Jews work its land and palms for half the produce while he wished; later Umar offered the Prophet's wives land or wasqs and expelled the Jews.
Whatever people, beasts or birds eat from what a Muslim plants or sows, or is stolen from it, counts as charity for him.
If fruit sold to a brother is struck by calamity the seller may take nothing; the Prophet ordered deductions for such loss and forbade selling dates before they ripen.
Creditors were told to take what a ruined debtor had, one who swore against granting remission relented, and at the Prophet's sign Ka'b remitted half of a debt.
A seller who finds his goods still intact with a buyer who has become insolvent has more right to them than any other creditor.
Allah forgave a rich man of earlier times who gave respite to insolvent debtors and leniency to the solvent; whoever wants safety on Resurrection Day should grant respite or remit.
A rich man's delay in paying a debt is injustice, and a creditor referred to a rich man for payment should accept the referral.
The Prophet forbade selling excess water or withholding it to hinder the growth of herbage, and forbade hiring out a camel for covering and selling land for tilling.
The Prophet forbade a dog's price, a prostitute's earnings and a soothsayer's fee, called the first two and a cupper's earnings evil, and disapproved of selling a dog or cat.
The Prophet ordered dogs in Medina killed, then forbade it except for the jet-black dog with two spots, and allowed dogs kept for hunting, herds and fields.
Whoever keeps a dog not needed for hunting or guarding herds or fields loses one or two qirat of his reward every day.
The Prophet was cupped, paid the cupper and had the cupper's dues lightened, calling cupping the best treatment; Ibn Abbas said he would not have paid an unlawful earning.
When Allah forbade wine the Prophet forbade drinking or selling it, and people poured it out in Medina; after Sura Baqara's last verses on riba he forbade trading in it.
In Mecca the Prophet forbade selling wine, carcasses, swine and idols, even carcass fat, and invoked Allah against the Jews, who melted fat forbidden to them and sold it.
Gold for gold and silver for silver are sold only like for like, without excess or delay; Umar stopped Talha deferring payment for gold, as deferred exchange is interest.
Gold, silver, wheat, barley, dates and salt are exchanged like for like and hand to hand, any excess being interest; Ubada b. Samit repeated this despite Mu'awiya.
Selling silver for gold on credit is usury; it is allowed only when payment is made on the spot, as al-Bara, Zaid b. Arqam and Abu Bakra reported.
A gold necklace with gems taken at Khaibar could be sold only after its gold was separated and weighed equally, and Ma'mar returned the excess barley received for wheat.
Exchanging two sa's of poor dates for one of fine dates is interest; the Prophet said to sell the poor dates for money and buy the fine ones with it.
Questioned by Abu Sa'id, Ibn Abbas said he had his view not from the Prophet or the Book but from Usama b. Zaid: interest lies in credit, not hand-to-hand exchange.
The Prophet cursed the one who takes interest, the one who pays it, the one who records it and its two witnesses, saying they are all equal.
The lawful and the unlawful are clear, with doubtful things between them; avoiding these keeps faith and honour blameless, and the body is sound when the heart is sound.
The Prophet prayed for Jabir's tired camel so that it ran, bought it letting him ride it to Medina, then paid him extra and gave him back the camel.
The Prophet repaid a borrowed young camel with an older, better one, saying the best people are those best at repaying debts and a creditor may speak out.
A slave pledged emigration to the Prophet, who did not know his status; he bought him from his master for two black slaves and afterwards asked before taking anyone's pledge.
The Prophet bought grain from a Jew on credit for a set time and gave him his iron coat of mail as a pledge.
Finding people in Medina paying a year or two in advance for fruit, the Prophet ruled that advance payment must be for a specified measure, weight and period.
Only a sinner hoards, the Prophet said; Sa'id b. al-Musayyib, told that he hoarded too, replied that Ma'mar who narrated it also hoarded.
Swearing in selling brings goods a quick sale but wipes out the blessing.
A partner in shared land, a house or a garden may not sell his share before offering it to his partner, who has the right of pre-emption.
No one should stop his neighbour from fixing a beam in his wall, and Abu Huraira rebuked those who turned away from this.
Whoever wrongly takes a span of land wears seven earths around his neck; Arwa, disputing land with Sa'id b. Zaid, went blind and fell into a pit, as he prayed.
When people disagree about a path, its width is to be seven cubits.
A Muslim and a non-Muslim do not inherit from each other; fixed shares go to those entitled under the Book of Allah, the rest to the nearest male heir.
The Prophet visited Jabir, unconscious with illness, and sprinkled his ablution water on him; asked about his property, he gave no reply until a verse on inheritance came down.
In a Friday sermon Umar said no problem troubled him more than kalala, for which the Prophet referred him to the summer verse ending Sura al-Nisa.
Al-Bara said the last verse revealed was the one on kalala and the last complete sura revealed was Sura Bara'at.
The Prophet, saying he is nearest to the believers, took on the debts and destitute children of those who died, while their property goes to their heirs.
Umar was told not to buy back the horse he gave in Allah's path even for a dirham; taking back charity or a gift is like a dog eating vomit.
Bashir asked the Prophet to witness his gift to his son Nu'man alone; he refused to witness injustice, told him to treat his children equally, and the gift was returned.
A life grant belongs to the recipient and his heirs, never returning to the giver unless given only for the recipient's lifetime; keep your property and do not squander it.
A garden given as a life grant stayed with the recipient's descendants after Jabir testified the Prophet said a life grant belongs to its recipient, and he called it permissible.
A Muslim with something to bequeath should not pass two or three nights without his will written down; Ibn Umar never spent a night without his after hearing this.
Ill in Mecca with one daughter as heir, Sa'd was allowed to bequeath a third, which is much; leaving heirs rich is better than leaving them begging.
Charity given for a parent who died without a will benefits them, and when a man dies his deeds end except ongoing charity, beneficial knowledge and a pious son's prayer.
Umar, advised by the Prophet, gave his Khaibar land as charity never to be sold, inherited or gifted, its produce for the poor, kin, freeing slaves, Allah's way and guests.
The Prophet left no wealth and made no will about property, only by the Book of Allah; Aisha denied any will for Ali, as the Prophet died in her lap.
When his illness worsened on a Thursday, the Prophet asked to write a guiding document; they disputed, Umar saying the Quran suffices, and the Prophet willed polytheists out of Arabia.
Sa'd b. Ubada was told to fulfil on his dead mother's behalf a vow she had died without fulfilling.
The Prophet forbade taking vows: a vow neither hastens nor delays anything nor averts what Allah has decreed; it only draws something out of the miser.
A captive was ransomed for two Muslims; an Ansari woman fleeing captivity on the Prophet's she-camel vowed to sacrifice it, but no vow holds in disobedience or beyond one's control.
An old man vowing to walk to the Ka'bah was told to ride, Allah needing no self-punishment, and Uqba's sister, vowing it barefoot, was told to walk and ride.
The expiation for breaking a vow is the same as the expiation for breaking an oath.
Swearing by one's fathers or by idols is forbidden: swear by Allah or keep silent, and whoever swears by Lat should say there is no god but Allah.
The Prophet swore he had no mounts for the Ash'arites, then gave them camels, saying Allah provided them and that he breaks an oath for something better and expiates it.
The Prophet swore he had no mounts for Abu Musa's companions, then gave them camels, saying that when he sees something better than an oath he does it and expiates.
Whoever swears an oath and finds something better should do that and expiate; Adi broke an oath for this, and Abd al-Rahman b. Samura was told not to seek authority.
An oath should be one that one's companion will believe, and it is interpreted according to the intention of the one who takes it.
Solomon said he would go round his wives in one night to beget horsemen for Allah's cause but did not say Insha' Allah, and only one bore an incomplete child.
Persisting in an oath concerning one's family is more sinful in Allah's sight than paying the expiation He imposed for breaking it.
Umar had vowed in the days of Ignorance to observe i'tikaf for a night or a day in the Sacred Mosque, and the Prophet told him to fulfil his vow.
Freeing a slave is the expiation for slapping or beating him without cause; the Prophet ordered the sons of Muqarrin to free their only slave-girl after one slapped her.
The Prophet warned Abu Mas'ud, who was beating his slave, that Allah had more power over him than he over the slave; freeing him spared Abu Mas'ud the Fire.
Whoever accuses his slave of adultery will be punished on the Day of Resurrection, unless the slave is as he said.
Abu Dharr dressed his slave like himself: the Prophet called slaves brothers, to be fed and clothed as their masters, not overburdened, and given some of the food they cook.
A slave who serves his master and worships Allah well has two rewards; but for jihad, Pilgrimage and his mother, Abu Huraira would have preferred to die a slave.
Whoever frees his share in a shared slave must, if able, pay to free him fully; otherwise the slave is partly freed or works for the rest without being overburdened.
When owners with no other property freed slaves at death, the Prophet freed only two of six by lot, and sold one declared free after his owner's death.
When Abdullah b. Sahl was found killed at Khaibar, his kin would neither swear fifty oaths nor accept the Jews' oaths, so the Prophet paid the blood-wit; he kept qasama.
Ukl or Uraina men, cured by camels' milk and urine, killed the shepherds, left Islam and drove off the camels; their hands and feet were cut and eyes put out.
A Jew who killed a girl for her ornaments, named by her nod and by his own confession, was killed with stones by the Prophet's order.
A man lost a front tooth when another pulled his bitten hand from his mouth, and the Prophet rejected his claim, asking whether he wished to bite like a camel.
When Umm Haritha broke a person's teeth the Prophet ordered retribution as in Allah's Book; Umm Rubayyi' swore it would not be taken, and the injured side accepted blood-wit.
A Muslim's blood is lawful only for married adultery, a life for a life, or leaving Islam; Adam's first son shares every unjust killing, and bloodshed is judged first.
On the Day of Sacrifice the Prophet named the four sacred months and declared lives, property and honour as sacred as that day, month and city.
The Prophet handed a man who confessed to killing to the victim's heir, saying that if he killed him he would be like him, and the heir let him go.
A woman struck another with a stone or tent-pole, killing her and her unborn child; the Prophet fixed a slave for the child and blood-wit on the striker's paternal kin.
The hand is cut for no less than a quarter dinar or a shield's price; the Prophet invoked Allah's curse on a thief losing it for an egg or rope.
When Usama interceded for a Makhzumi woman who stole, the Prophet rebuked him, saying earlier peoples perished by sparing the noble, and that he would cut even Fatima's hand.
Allah ordained that unmarried adulterers receive a hundred lashes and a year's exile and married ones a hundred lashes and stoning; Umar said the verse of stoning was sent down.
Ma'iz b. Malik confessed adultery four times; after asking about his sanity and marriage the Prophet had him stoned, then threatened whoever lagged behind on expeditions bleating like a he-goat.
Ma'iz and women of Ghamid and Juhaina asked to be purified of adultery; the women were stoned after giving birth, and the Prophet prayed over them, praising their repentance.
Jews guilty of adultery were stoned once the Torah's verse of stoning, which they had set aside, came out; Ibn Abu Aufa did not know whether stoning preceded Sura al-Nur.
A slave-woman who commits adultery is flogged without reproach and sold after repeated offences; Ali delayed flogging one who had just given birth, and the Prophet approved.
The Prophet and Abu Bakr gave a wine drinker forty strokes and Umar eighty; Ali had Walid lashed forty, and would pay indemnity for a drunkard dying under punishment.
No one is to be given more than ten lashes except in one of Allah's prescribed punishments.
The companions pledged, like the women, not to associate anything with Allah, steal, commit adultery or kill; a punished sin is expiated, and one Allah conceals is left to Him.
No compensation is due for injury caused by an animal or by falling into a well or a mine, and a fifth is due on buried treasure.
The defendant must take the oath, for otherwise people would claim others' lives and property, and the Prophet also judged on an oath with a witness.
The Prophet said he judges disputes by what he hears, so whoever is given his brother's right by his ruling is given a portion of the Fire.
Hind told the Prophet her husband Abu Sufyan was miserly, and he allowed her to take from his wealth what was reasonable and sufficient for herself and her children.

Allah likes worship without partners and holding fast to His rope, forbids disobeying mothers, burying daughters alive and withholding rights, and dislikes idle talk, persistent questioning and wasting wealth.
A judge who strives and is right has two rewards and one who strives and errs has one, and no one should judge between two people while angry.
Innovating in the Prophet's affairs without valid reason, or doing any act without his sanction, is to be rejected.
The best witness is the one who gives his evidence before he is asked for it.
When a wolf took one of two women's sons, David judged for the elder, but Solomon, calling for a knife to divide the child, judged for the younger, who refused.
Buyer and seller of land both refused gold found in it, so their judge married one's son to the other's daughter and told them to spend and give charity.
Found property is announced for a year, its bag and strap noted, then used and repaid if the owner comes; a stray sheep may be taken, a camel left alone.
No one may milk another's animal without his permission, for its udders are its owner's store of food, as a storeroom no one would want broken into.
Guests are owed a day and night of special kindness and three days' hospitality, beyond that charity, must not exhaust their host, and may take their due when refused.
On a journey the Prophet told those with a spare mount or surplus provisions to give them to those without, and named many other kinds of wealth likewise.
Pooled on a small sheet at the Prophet's command, scarce expedition provisions fed fourteen hundred people, who filled their bags, and a small bucket of water sufficed their ablution.
Inviting the enemy to Islam was needed early on, and Banu Mustaliq were raided unawares; commanders were to offer Islam, emigration or jizya before fighting, never mutilating or killing children.
Sending companions on missions, including Mu'adh to Yemen, the Prophet told them to give glad tidings, be lenient and not harsh, and not create aversion.
On the Day of Judgment every perfidious person will have a flag proclaiming his treachery, raised in proportion to it, and no treachery is greater than that of a ruler.
War is a stratagem; do not wish to meet the enemy but ask Allah for safety, and when you meet them be firm: Paradise is under the shadows of swords.
The Prophet asked Allah, Revealer of the Book, to rout and shake the tribes, and at Uhud said if Allah willed, none would be left on earth to worship Him.
Finding a woman killed in battle, the Prophet forbade killing women and children; asked about polytheists' women and children struck in night raids, he said they are from them.
The Prophet had the date-palms of Banu Nadir at Buwaira cut down and burnt, and a verse came saying that trees cut or left standing were by Allah's permission.
An earlier prophet's spoils were consumed by fire once misappropriated gold was returned, spoils being lawful only for this community; Sa'd's request for a sword brought the verse on spoils.
Troops sent to Najd got twelve camels each and one extra; the Prophet gave small detachments more than a share in a large force, the fifth always being reserved.
The Prophet gave an enemy's belongings to his killer, as to Abu Qatada, one of Abu Jahl's slayers and Salama, but backed Khalid against a claim after Auf taunted him.
Abu Bakr gave Salama a captive girl taken from Fazara, and the Prophet asked him for her and sent her to Mecca as ransom for Muslims held prisoner there.
A township gained without war gives its takers a share, a fighting one a fifth to Allah and His Messenger; Banu Nadir's property, gained without fighting, was the Prophet's own.
Prophets leave no heirs, their legacy being charity, so Abu Bakr refused Fatima her share and Umar held Abbas and Ali to it; Ali later pledged allegiance to Abu Bakr.
The Prophet said his heirs would not share even a dinar of what he left: after his wives' maintenance and his manager's pay, all he leaves is charity.
The Prophet gave a horseman two shares of the spoils and a footman one.
At Badr Allah answers the Prophet's prayer with angels; he takes ransom for captives on Abu Bakr's advice, weeps at the punishment shown for it, and booty is made lawful.
Thumama b. Uthal, a captured chief of Yamama, is held bound in the mosque, questioned thrice, then freed by the Prophet; he bathes, embraces Islam and goes on to Umrah.
The Prophet calls the Jews to Islam, warning of expulsion; Banu Nadir are expelled, Quraiza's men killed after they fought, and he vows to expel Jews and Christians from Arabia.
Banu Quraiza surrender to Sa'd b. Mu'adh's judgment that their fighters be killed and families captured; Sa'd dies when his wound reopens, and companions differ over praying before reaching Quraiza.
The Ansar shared their orchards with the penniless Muhajirs, who returned these gifts after later conquests; the Prophet gave Umm Aiman, who had nursed him, other palms for those returned.
On the day of Khaibar Abdullah b. Mughaffal seized a bag of fat, vowing to give none of it away, then turned to find the Prophet smiling and felt ashamed.
Heraclius questions Abu Sufyan about the Prophet, then reads his letter inviting him to Islam; the Prophet also wrote inviting Chosroes, the Negus and every other ruler to Allah.
At Hunain the Muslims fall back before archers while the Prophet holds firm on his white mule; Abbas calls them back, and he throws pebbles at the enemy, who flee.
The Prophet besieges Ta'if without taking it; his companions resist leaving, a morning raid leaves them wounded, and they gladly depart the next day as he laughs.
Before Badr the Prophet consults his companions and Sa'd b. Ubada pledges to follow him anywhere; a captured water-carrier is beaten, and the Prophet marks where each enemy will fall.
Taking Mecca, the Prophet assures the Ansar he will live and die with them, strikes the idols round the Ka'bah, and says no Quraishite will henceforth be killed bound.
Ali writes the Hudaybiyya treaty and the Prophet himself strikes out 'Messenger of Allah', accepting the Meccans' terms; Umar objects, and a surah of victory is revealed.
Hudhaifa and his father, caught by Quraish on the way to Badr, promised not to fight with the Prophet, who told them to keep that promise and seek Allah's help.
On a bitterly cold, windy night of Ahzab the Prophet sends Hudhaifa to bring news of the enemy without provoking them; he holds back from shooting Abu Sufyan and returns.
At Uhud Ansar die defending the wounded Prophet, whose bleeding Fatima stops; he asks how his attackers can be saved, and recalls a prophet who asked forgiveness for his people.
Quraish lay a camel's foetus on the prostrating Prophet and he invokes Allah against their chiefs, later slain at Badr; rejected at Aqaba, he spares his people; his finger bleeds.
When Gabriel delayed and the Prophet, ill, did not rise for night prayer, polytheists said he was forsaken, and Allah revealed that his Lord had not forsaken him.
Abdullah b. Ubayy rebuffs the Prophet's call and the two sides quarrel; the Prophet calms them and forgives him, and a verse on making peace between quarrelling believers comes.
After Badr Ibn Mas'ud finds Abu Jahl dying, struck down by the two sons of Afra, and Abu Jahl laments that farmers killed him.
The Prophet asks who will kill Ka'b b. Ashraf for maligning Allah and His Messenger; Muhammad b. Maslama draws him out with a loan ruse and his party kills him.
The Prophet raids Khaibar at dawn, foretelling its ruin, and takes it; Amir b. al-Akwa', the march's poet, dies by his own sword yet has a double reward.
Carrying earth while digging the ditch, the Prophet chants verses with his companions, praying that, since true life is the Hereafter's, Allah forgive and help the Ansar and Muhajirs.
Salama b. al-Akwa' pledges allegiance thrice at Hudaybiyya, recovers the Prophet's camels from raiders at Dhu Qarad alone and sees Ali take Khaibar; attacking Meccans are captured and spared.
Umm Sulaim bears a dagger at Hunain; Ansar women go to war to give water and treat the wounded; at Uhud Abu Talha shields the Prophet while women carry water.
Ibn Abbas answers Najda: women and slaves get booty gifts, not shares; enemy children are not killed; orphanhood ends at maturity; the fifth for the Prophet's kin was denied them.
Umm Atiyya took part in seven battles with the Prophet, staying in the camp to cook, treat the wounded and nurse the sick.
Companions count the Prophet's expeditions, nineteen by several reports with fighting in eight, and Abu Musa tells how the Dhat ar-Riqa' expedition was named for their rag-bound feet.
On the way to Badr the Prophet twice turns away a brave polytheist seeking to join for booty, taking no help from a polytheist, and accepts him once he believes.
People follow the Quraish in good and evil, the Caliphate stays with them, and Islam remains strong until twelve caliphs, all from Quraish, have ruled.
Wounded, Umar indicates he will name no successor, as the Prophet named none though Abu Bakr did, despite his son's warning that the people would be left untended.
The Prophet says not to ask for authority and appoints none who seek it; Abu Dharr is weak, and office is a trust bringing regret on Judgement Day unless fulfilled.
The just will sit on pulpits of light near Allah, and the Prophet prayed that Allah be hard on rulers hard on his people and kind to the kind.
Everyone is a shepherd answerable for his flock; a ruler who dies cheating or neglecting his people is barred from Paradise, and the cruel ruler is the worst.
Whoever misappropriates booty or public funds, even a needle, will carry it on Judgement Day; an official who claimed as his own gifts given him while collecting charity is rebuked.
The verse on obeying those in authority came about a commander the Prophet sent; whoever obeys the Prophet obeys Allah, and whoever obeys his commander obeys him.
Muslims must listen to and obey the ruler in hardship and ease, even when others are preferred, and even a maimed Abyssinian slave who leads by Allah's Book.
Obedience to a ruler holds except in sin: those who refused a commander's order to enter a fire were right; companions pledged to obey in all conditions save clear disbelief.
The ruler is a shield; many caliphs will follow the Prophet, the first given allegiance taking precedence; amid coming trials one obeys them, but not in disobeying Allah.
An Ansari who asked for office was told to bear favouritism after the Prophet patiently until the Cistern; rulers who withhold people's rights must be obeyed, each bearing his burden.
Hudhaifa asked about evil times ahead; the Prophet foretold callers at Hell's gates and leaders not following his guidance, and said to keep with the Muslims' main body and Amir.
Whoever leaves obedience and the main body, dies with no oath of allegiance, or is killed under a blind banner for his tribe dies the death of Jahiliyya.
Whoever seeks to split the community united under one leader is to be killed, and when allegiance is given to two caliphs, the later one is to be killed.
Rulers will do good and bad: whoever hates their wrongs is blameless, whoever approves them is ruined, and while they establish prayer, none may fight them or withdraw obedience.
At Hudaibiya thirteen to fifteen hundred pledged allegiance under the tree, not to die fighting but never to flee; the Prophet called them the best people on earth.
Next year those who pledged could not find the tree; Salama said they pledged to die fighting, and Abdullah b. Zaid would make no such pledge after the Prophet.
No emigration remains after the conquest of Mecca, only jihad and intention; the Prophet let Salama live in the desert and told a Bedouin paying zakat to keep doing good.
The Prophet took the pledge of the believing women who emigrated by spoken word on the terms of the Quranic verse, and his hand never touched a woman's hand.
Companions pledged to the Prophet to hear and obey, and he had them add: as far as it lies in my power.
Ibn Umar was turned away from fighting at Uhud aged fourteen and allowed at the Trench aged fifteen, which Umar b. Abd al-Aziz made the line between minor and adult.
The Prophet forbade travelling to enemy land with the Quran, fearing it would fall into the enemy's hands.
The Prophet held races for trained and untrained horses, and said that good, reward and booty are tied to the forelocks of horses until the Day of Judgement.
The Prophet disliked the shikal horse, explained as one with a white hind foot and the opposite white forefoot.
Allah guarantees whoever fights in His way Paradise or return with reward and booty; his wound will smell of musk, and the Prophet longed to be killed again and again.
No one in Paradise would wish to return to this world except the martyr, who wishes to return and be killed ten times for the honour he has seen.
Jihad equals ceaseless fasting and prayer and ranks above serving pilgrims; a morning or evening of it outweighs the world, and it raises a man a hundred grades in Paradise.
One killed in Allah's way, patient, sincere and never fleeing, is forgiven all but debt; martyrs' souls live in green birds eating Paradise's fruit and ask to be slain again.
The best man fights in Allah's way with life and wealth; next is one living apart in a mountain valley, worshipping his Lord and sparing people his harm.
Allah laughs at two men entering Paradise, a martyr and his killer who later embraces Islam and is martyred; a disbeliever and his believing killer never meet in Hell.
A muzzled she-camel given in Allah's way earns seven hundred; guiding someone to a mount earns the doer's reward; equipping a fighter or caring for his family counts as fighting.
Those caring for the families of fighters sent against Banu Lihyan share their reward; whoever betrays a fighter's family yields his deeds to him, and the disabled are excused.
Men who heard of Paradise fought until killed, among them Umair b. al-Humam at Badr and Anas's uncle at Uhud; the seventy slain Reciters were pleased with their Lord.
Asked about fighting for booty, fame, valour, rage or family pride, the Prophet said whoever fights so that Allah's word is exalted fights in Allah's way.
The first judged will be a man killed fighting, a scholar and reciter, and a rich giver, all cast into Hell for acting to be called brave, learned and generous.
Fighters who return safe with booty have received two-thirds of their reward in advance, while those who return empty-handed or wounded receive their full reward.
Deeds count by intention; sincerely seeking martyrdom ranks one among martyrs, those kept home by illness share the reward, and dying without fighting or wishing to is a hypocrite's death.
Waking from a nap laughing, the Prophet said he was shown followers sailing the sea to fight like kings on thrones, and told Umm Haram she was among the first.
A day and night on watch beats a month of fasting and night prayer; whoever dies at it earns its reward forever and is spared the grave's torment.
Those who die of plague or diarrhoea, drown, are buried under debris or die in Allah's way are martyrs; Allah forgave a man for moving a thorny twig aside.
Strength lies in archery, which none should give up even once lands are opened; one who learns it and then abandons it is not of us.
A group of the Prophet's Umma will remain triumphant on the truth, unharmed by opponents, until the Hour; a musk-scented wind will then take every believer, leaving only the worst.
On journeys let camels graze in fertile land, hurry through barren land and do not camp on the road at night; travel is a hardship, so hurry home when done.
The Prophet did not return home by night and forbade travellers to surprise their families at night, suspecting or spying on them, so that wives could first groom themselves.
Game from a trained dog sent with Allah's name is lawful unless it ate or another dog joined; game hit flat by a blunt arrow, or found drowned, is not.
The People of the Book's vessels may be used, washed, only when no others exist; game taken with Allah's name may be eaten even three days later if not rotten.
The Prophet forbade eating any fanged beast of prey and any bird with talons.
Three hundred men under Abu Ubaida, reduced to a date a day and leaves, ate for weeks from a whale the sea cast up, and the Prophet ate some.
At Khaibar the Prophet forbade temporary marriage and domestic asses' flesh, and pots were overturned; companions differed whether the ban was permanent or due to the unpaid fifth.
At Khaibar the flesh of domestic asses was declared impure and its pots overturned or broken, while horse meat was permitted and eaten in the Prophet's lifetime.
Asked about the lizard, the Prophet said he neither ate it nor forbade it; it is lawful, but not his food.
At Maimuna's house the Prophet drew back from a roasted lizard, not found in his people's land, but let Khalid b. Walid and others eat it at his table.
Not knowing whether the lizard came from a Bani Isra'il tribe transformed into beasts, the Prophet neither ate nor forbade it; Umar said it was shepherds' common food.
Companions ate locusts on six or seven expeditions with the Prophet, and he accepted a share of a hare that Abu Talha slaughtered.
The Prophet forbade flinging pebbles, which neither catch game nor defeat an enemy but break teeth and put out eyes; Ibn Mughaffal would not speak to one who persisted.
Allah has enjoined goodness in everything: kill well, slaughter well, sharpen the knife and let the slaughtered animal die at ease.
The Prophet forbade tying up animals or any living thing as a target for arrows, cursed whoever does so, and forbade killing a beast after it has been tied.
An animal slaughtered before the Eid al-Adha prayer is only meat and must be replaced; Abu Burda, who slaughtered early, was allowed a young goat, but none after him.
Slaughtering before the prayer or the Prophet's sacrifice must be repeated; a grown animal is sacrificed, or a young sheep when that is hard; Uqba was allowed a young lamb.
The Prophet sacrificed two horned rams with his own hand, naming and glorifying Allah, and over another ram asked Allah to accept it from Muhammad, his family and Umma.
Facing the enemy without knives, companions were told to slaughter with anything that makes blood flow, naming Allah, but not tooth or nail, and to shoot a camel that bolts.
The Prophet forbade eating sacrificial meat beyond three days when needy people had come, then allowed eating, storing and giving it in charity once that hardship passed.
On the Farewell Pilgrimage the Prophet had Thauban prepare the meat of his sacrifice to last, and he ate from it until he reached Medina.
The Prophet said there is no Fara' and no 'Atira, Fara' being explained as the first-born of a camel.
The Prophet lifted three earlier bans: graves may be visited, sacrificial meat kept as long as wished, and Nabidh made in any vessel, but not drunk once it intoxicates.
One who intends to sacrifice should not cut his hair or trim his nails once Dhu'l-Hijja begins; Sa'id b. al-Musayyib called this a forgotten, abandoned hadith.
Denying the Prophet told him secrets, Ali cited four whom Allah cursed: one who sacrifices to other than Allah, curses his parents, shelters an innovator or moves land boundaries.
While drunk, Hamza cut up Ali's two she-camels, meant to fund his wedding feast with Fatima; reproached by the Prophet, Hamza answered as one intoxicated, and the Prophet withdrew.
When liquor was declared unlawful, Anas poured away the date liquor he was serving, and it flowed through Medina's lanes; in those days their liquor was made from dates.
Wine may not be turned into vinegar and is no medicine but an ailment; the Prophet said wine comes from two trees, the date-palm and the vine.
The Prophet forbade making Nabidh by mixing two fruits, such as fresh dates with grapes or with unripe dates, and said to prepare each kind separately.
The Prophet forbade mixing dates with grapes, or unripe with dry dates, for Nabidh, told people to prepare each separately, and wrote to the people of Jurash forbidding it.
The Prophet forbade preparing Nabidh in gourds, varnished jars, green pitch-coated pitchers and hollow stumps, telling the Abd al-Qais delegation to use small waterskins tied at the mouth.
The Prophet forbade the Abd al-Qais delegation and others to prepare Nabidh in gourds, pitch-coated pitchers, hollow stumps and varnished jars, and forbade mixing ripe with nearly ripe dates.
Asked repeatedly, Ibn Umar confirmed the Prophet's ban on Nabidh in pitch-coated pitchers, gourds, varnished jars and hollowed palm stumps, explaining the terms, and his command to use waterskins.
The Prophet forbade Nabidh in green pitchers, varnished jars and hollow stumps; it was prepared for him in a waterskin, or in a stone bowl when none was found.
The Prophet lifted his ban on vessels, saying no vessel makes a drink lawful or unlawful but every intoxicant is forbidden, and allowed green pitchers not coated with pitch.
Asked about Bit' from honey and Mizr from barley or millet, the Prophet said every intoxicant is forbidden, and Allah will give drinkers of intoxicants the sweat of Hell's inmates.
Every intoxicant is Khamr and every intoxicant is forbidden; whoever drinks wine in this world and does not repent will be deprived of it in the Hereafter.
Nabidh steeped for the Prophet in a waterskin was drunk for up to three days, the rest given away or poured out; Ibn Abbas said wine may not be traded.
At Abu Usaid's wedding feast his bride served the Prophet dates she had steeped overnight in a stone bowl, giving it to him after he had eaten.
An Arab woman the Prophet came to propose to sought refuge with Allah from him, not knowing him, and he left her; then Sahl served him drink from a cup.
Anas served the Prophet honey, Nabidh, water and milk in his own cup.
Going from Mecca to Medina, Abu Bakr milked for the thirsty Prophet at a shepherd's; Suraqa's horse sank at the Prophet's curse, and on Suraqa's plea he prayed for him.
On the night journey, offered wine and milk, the Prophet took the milk; Gabriel said he was guided to the true nature and wine would have misled his Umma.
The Prophet asked why cups of milk and Nabidh brought to him were uncovered, even by a stick laid across; waterskins were to be tied and doors closed at night.
Cover vessels, tie waterskins, shut doors naming Allah, and put out lamps and fires at night; keep children in at nightfall when Satan roams; a yearly pestilence enters uncovered vessels.
Satan claims food over which Allah's name is not mentioned and eats with his left hand; mention Allah, eat and drink with the right hand, and eat what is near.
The Prophet forbade drinking from the mouth of an upturned waterskin and drinking while standing, saying one who forgets should vomit, yet he drank Zamzam standing near the House.
The Prophet forbade breathing into the vessel and drank in three breaths, passing drink to the one on his right: a desert Arab over Abu Bakr, a boy over elders.
The Prophet licked his three fingers after eating; lick fingers and dish, for the blessing's place is unknown, and clean and eat a dropped morsel, not leaving it for Satan.
Hosts allowed an uninvited follower and, at the Prophet's insistence, Aisha to join; an Ansari feasted the hungry Prophet, Abu Bakr and Umar, a bounty they will be questioned about.
At the ditch the Prophet blessed Jabir's lamb and barley and a thousand ate; at Abu Talha's he blessed some loaves and seventy or eighty ate, with food left over.
The Prophet relished pumpkin at a tailor's meal, ate dates holding stones between his fingers and prayed for his host, and ate cucumber with fresh dates, and dates while squatting.
The Prophet forbade taking two dates at once without one's companions' consent, and said a household that has dates will not be hungry.
Seven morning ajwa dates protect from poison and magic that day; truffles are a kind of manna Allah sent the people of Israel, their juice medicine for the eyes.
Picking arak fruit at Marr az-Zahran, the Prophet advised taking the black ones and confirmed he had shepherded a flock, asking whether any prophet had not done so.
Asking his household for a condiment and told there was only vinegar, the Prophet ate bread with it and said vinegar is a good condiment, which made Jabir love vinegar.
The Prophet left food with garlic untouched, telling his host Abu Ayyub it was not forbidden but he disliked its odour, so Abu Ayyub disliked it too.
An Ansari couple fed the Prophet's guest in the dark, putting their children to sleep, and a verse came down; the Prophet hosted the starving Miqdad and two companions.
With 130 companions, the Prophet bought a polytheist's sheep, shared its roasted liver with everyone, and two bowls of it fed them all with some left over.
Abu Bakr hosted poor people of Suffa; returning late, he found they had refused to eat without him, swore off food, saw the food multiply, then ate.
Food for one suffices two, food for two suffices three or four, and food for four suffices eight.
A believer eats in one intestine and a non-believer in seven; a non-Muslim guest drank seven goats' milk, then after accepting Islam could not finish a second.
The Prophet never found fault with food; if he liked it he ate it, and if not he left it or kept silent.
Whoever eats or drinks from vessels of gold or silver drinks down the fire of Hell into his belly.

The Prophet commanded visiting the sick, following funerals, answering sneezers, fulfilling vows, helping the poor, accepting invitations and greeting, and forbade gold rings, silver vessels, silk saddle cloths and silk.
Hudhaifa rejected a silver vessel, citing the Prophet's ban on gold and silver vessels and silk, which are for non-believers in this world and for you in the Hereafter.
Refusing Utarid's silk robe, the Prophet said its wearer has no share in the Hereafter, then sent silk to Umar and others to sell or cut into women's head coverings.
Asma' showed the Prophet's brocade-bordered cloak, Ibn Zubair forbade dressing women in silk, and Umar conveyed that the Prophet allowed silk only two to four fingers wide.
The Prophet took off gifted silk, saying Gabriel forbade it and it does not befit the Godfearing, giving it to Umar to sell and Ali to cut for women.
The Prophet allowed Abd al-Rahman b. Auf and Zubair to wear silk shirts because of itch or lice, including on a journey.
The Prophet called saffron-dyed clothes non-believers' dress, told Abdullah b. Amr to burn his, and forbade Ali silk, yellow clothes, gold rings and reciting Quran when bowing or prostrating.
The Prophet liked the Yemeni mantle best, died in coarse garments, wore a black hair blanket with saddle patterns, and his pillow and bedding were leather stuffed with palm fibre.
When Jabir married, the Prophet said he would soon have carpets, and his wife cited this to keep one; bedding is for husband, wife and guest, a fourth for Satan.
Allah will not look on the Day of Resurrection at whoever trails his garment out of pride, as Ibn Umar told a man of Laith he saw trailing his.
The Prophet had Ibn Umar raise his garment to mid-shank; Abu Huraira cited the hadith at a strutting Amir; a man proud of his mantles sank into the earth.
The Prophet forbade gold rings as live coals from Hell and discarded his own; his silver ring engraved 'Muhammad, Messenger of Allah' passed to Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman.
The Prophet had a silver seal ring made for letters to kings, wore it with its Abyssinian stone inward, and the people copied him in wearing and discarding rings.
The Prophet forbade Ali to wear a ring on his middle finger or the one beside it, and forbade Qassi silk garments and red silk saddle cloths.
Wear sandals, for the wearer is like a rider; put on the right first, remove the left first, and never walk in one sandal, even with a broken thong.
The Prophet forbade eating left-handed, walking in one sandal, wrapping oneself with no opening for the arms, and sitting with a single garment wrapped round the knees, which may expose.
Lying on one's back with one foot over the other was forbidden, yet the Prophet was seen lying that way in the mosque.
The Prophet forbade saffron dye, had Abu Quhafa's white hair changed at the Conquest of Mecca, avoiding black, and said to oppose Jews and Christians, who do not dye.
Gabriel kept away over a puppy under the Prophet's cot: angels do not enter a house with a dog or picture; a carpet Aisha hung over her door was torn.
The Prophet had Aisha remove curtains with portraits, tearing some and saying those who imitate Allah's creation face the severest torment; she made cushions from them, which he reclined on.
Picture-makers will be most severely tormented on the Day of Resurrection, told to breathe souls into their works; Ibn Abbas told a painter to paint trees and lifeless things instead.
Angels do not accompany travellers who have a dog and a bell, the bell being Satan's instrument, and the Prophet ordered string necklaces removed from camels' necks.
The Prophet forbade striking or branding animals' faces, saying Allah cursed whoever branded an ass's face, and branded animals on the buttocks or ears, including Zakat camels.
The Prophet forbade Qaza', shaving part of a boy's head and leaving part unshaven.
Those who must sit on the paths should give the path its rights: lowering the gaze, causing no harm, exchanging greetings, and commanding good and forbidding evil.
Asked about false hair for a bride who lost hers, the Prophet cursed the woman who adds false hair and the one who asks for it, and one seeking tattoos.
Allah cursed women who tattoo, pluck facial hair or space teeth, altering His creation, Abdullah told Umm Ya'qub; Mu'awiya cited the Prophet: false hair ruined the Israelites and is cheating.
The Prophet described two kinds of Hell's people he had not seen: people beating others with whips like ox tails, and women dressed yet naked who will not enter Paradise.
A wife who claims her husband gave her what he did not, to impress a co-wife, is like one wearing a garment of falsehood.
People may take the Prophet's name Muhammad but not his kunya Abu'l-Qasim, for he is the one who distributes; the names dearest to Allah are Abdullah and Abd al-Rahman.
Questioned in Najran about Mary being called sister of Harun though Moses long preceded Jesus, Mughira asked the Prophet, who said people were named after earlier prophets and pious people.
The Prophet forbade naming servants Aflah, Rabah, Yasar or Nafi', named the four phrases dearest to Allah, and, Jabir says, considered banning such names but did not.
The Prophet changed names such as Asiya to Jamila and Barra to Juwairiya or Zainab, saying do not claim piety; the vilest name before Allah is King of Kings.
The Prophet rubbed newborns' palates with dates he had chewed, blessed them and named them, including Abdullah b. Abi Talha, Ibrahim, Abdullah b. Zubair born at Quba, and Mundhir.
Anas said the Prophet had the finest character: he asked young Abu Umair what his sparrow had done, and he addressed Anas as 'my son'.
Mughira asked most about the Dajjal; the Prophet called him 'my son', said the Dajjal would not harm him and is more insignificant to Allah than his rivers and bread.
Abu Musa left Umar's door after asking permission three times unanswered, as the Prophet taught; Umar demanded a witness, and Abu Sa'id, the youngest present, testified for him.
Permission is sought three times, then one goes back; Umar demanded a witness from Abu Musa, and Abu Sa'id and Ubayy ibn Ka'b confirmed the Prophet said it.
When Jabir sought permission and answered the Prophet's question of who it was with 'It is I', the Prophet came out repeating 'It is I' as if disapproving.
Permission guards against glances; the Prophet said he would have pierced the eye of a man peeping through his door, and a household may put out an uninvited peeper's eyes.
Jarir asked the Prophet about a sudden glance, and he commanded him to turn his eyes away.
The rider greets the walker, the walker greets the one seated, and the small group greets the larger.
The Prophet told people to avoid sitting on the paths or else give them their rights: lowering the gaze, causing no harm, returning greetings, good talk, commanding good, forbidding evil.
A Muslim owes his brother five or six rights: returning his greeting, accepting his invitation, giving advice when asked, answering his sneeze, visiting him when ill and following his bier.
The People of the Book are answered 'And upon you', since some Jews greeted with 'Death be upon you'; when Aisha cursed them back, the Prophet said Allah loves kindness.
The Prophet said not to greet the Jews and Christians first, and when meeting one of them on the road, to force him to its narrowest part.
The Prophet greeted the boys he passed, and Anas and Thabit after him did the same.
The Prophet told Ibn Mas'ud that a raised curtain, or hearing his quiet talk, was the sign he could come in until told otherwise.
Umar called out to the tall Sauda when the Prophet's wives went out for their needs; revelation followed, in one report permitting them out, in another the veil verses.
No man may stay the night with a married woman but her husband or mahram, the husband's brother is like death, and none should enter an absent man's house alone.
Seen with a wife, once Safiyya visiting his i'tikaf, the Prophet told passers-by who she was, as Satan circulates in man like blood and might put evil in their hearts.
Of three men reaching the Prophet's circle, one took a gap and Allah sheltered him, one sat behind from shyness, and one left, so Allah turned away from him.
No one may make another rise to take his seat, even on Friday, but should say 'make room'; one who leaves his place and returns has most right to it.
A eunuch who visited the Prophet's household described a woman's body, so the Prophet said such men should not enter upon the women, who then veiled themselves from him.
Asma bint Abu Bakr did the work of Zubair's house and horse until given a servant, and felt shy, recalling Zubair's jealousy, when the Prophet offered her a ride.
When three are together, two should not converse secretly apart from the third until others join, for it grieves him.
Gabriel recited protection over the ill Prophet from envy and the evil eye, which the Prophet said is real, telling anyone asked to bathe for it to bathe.
Labid ibn al-A'sam of Banu Zuraiq cast a spell on the Prophet; answering his supplication, Allah informed him through two men that it lay in a well and cured him.
A Jewish woman brought the Prophet poisoned meat to kill him; he ate some, told her Allah would never let her, and refused his Companions' request to kill her.
The Prophet supplicated over the sick, rubbing them with his right hand and blowing the Mu'awwidhatan over them, and Aisha did so for him in his last illness.
The Prophet permitted incantation against poison, scorpion stings, pustules and the evil eye, and used dust and saliva, with Allah's name, as a cure.
Having forbidden incantation, the Prophet allowed it against snake and scorpion poison and the evil eye once he heard the words, saying there is no harm in incantation without polytheism.
A Companion cured a scorpion-stung tribal chief by reciting al-Fatiha and was given sheep; the Prophet asked how he knew it was an incantation and asked for a share.
For bodily pain the Prophet taught saying Bismillah thrice and seeking refuge in Allah's power seven times, and for the devil Khinzab confusing prayer, seeking refuge and spitting left thrice.

Every disease has a remedy by Allah's permission; the Prophet named cupping, honey and cauterisation though disliking cautery himself, cauterised wounded Companions, and was cupped and paid the cupper.
Fever comes from the raging heat of Hell, so cool it with water, as Asma did by sprinkling water at a feverish woman's collar.
In his illness the Prophet gestured against medicine poured into his mouth, and on recovering ordered it poured into the mouths of all except Ibn Abbas, who had been absent.
The Prophet told Umm Qais not to press her infant's uvula but use Indian aloeswood, which holds seven remedies including one for pleurisy, and sprinkled water on the boy's urine.
Nigella seed is a remedy for every disease except death, talbina comforts a grieving heart, and honey, given repeatedly, cured a man's loose bowels, for Allah spoke the truth.
Plague is a calamity sent on the Children of Israel or earlier peoples; do not enter a land where it breaks out, nor flee one where you are.
At Sargh, told of plague in Syria, Umar consulted the emigrants, Ansar and Quraysh elders and turned back, from Divine Decree to Divine Decree, as Abd al-Rahman's report confirmed.
The Prophet denied transitive disease, evil omens, safar, hama and ghoul, asking who infected the first camel, and also said the sick should not be brought to the healthy.
There is no transitive disease and no divination, but the Prophet liked the good omen, which is a good word that one hears.
If bad luck exists in anything, the Prophet said, it is in the house, the woman and the horse, or in one report the land, the servant and the horse.
Asked about pre-Islamic practices, the Prophet forbade visiting soothsayers, said omens should not hold one back, and allowed line-drawing only if it matches that of a prophet who drew lines.
Soothsayers' true words are snatched by a jinn and passed to his friend mixed with a hundred lies; angels pelt such jinn with meteors, which mark no birth or death.
Whoever visits a diviner and asks him about anything has his prayers of forty nights not accepted.
The Prophet sent word to a leper in the Thaqif delegation that his allegiance was accepted and he could go.
The Prophet ordered striped and short-tailed snakes killed, as they harm eyesight and cause miscarriage, but Abu Lubaba told Ibn Umar he forbade killing snakes that live in houses.
In a cave, as al-Mursalat was revealed, a snake escaped the Prophet's order to kill it, and he commanded a pilgrim in ihram to kill a snake at Mina.
A newly-wed man died after spearing a snake at home; the Prophet said Medina has Muslim jinn, so such snakes are warned for three days, then killed if seen again.
The Prophet ordered geckos killed, calling them little noxious creatures, with the greatest reward for killing one with the first blow and less for the second and third.
An earlier prophet, bitten by one ant, had the whole ant colony burnt, and Allah rebuked him for burning a community that glorified Him instead of killing the one ant.
A woman was thrown into Hell for keeping a cat tied until it starved, while a man and a prostitute were pardoned for giving water to a thirsty dog.
Allah says the son of Adam hurts Him by cursing Time, for He is Time, alternating night and day; nor should grapes be called karm, for karm is the believer.
None should say 'my bondman' or 'my slave-girl', for all are Allah's bondmen, nor call a master 'my lord', nor say 'my soul has become evil'.
Musk, put by a woman of the Children of Israel in her ring, is the best scent; a flower offered should not be refused, and the Prophet fumigated with aloeswood.
The Prophet heard a hundred couplets of Umayya ibn Abu Salt, who was almost a Muslim, and called Labid's verse that all but Allah is vain the truest poetry.
A belly filled with pus is better than a mind stuffed with poetry, the Prophet said, and at Arj he called a reciting poet a satan to be seized.
Whoever plays nardashir, a game like backgammon, is like one who dyes his hand with the flesh and blood of swine.
Good dreams are from Allah and bad ones from Satan; for a bad dream one spits left thrice, seeks refuge and tells no one, and it does no harm.
A believer's dream is a forty-sixth part of prophecy, in some reports a forty-fifth or seventieth; dreams are good tidings, Satan's distress or one's own thoughts.
Whoever sees the Prophet in a dream has truly seen him, for Satan cannot take his form.
When a desert Arab dreamt he was beheaded and chased his head, the Prophet told him not to relate Satan's play with him in sleep.
Abu Bakr interpreted a dream of a canopy dripping butter and honey and a rope to heaven; the Prophet said he was partly right and partly wrong.
The Prophet told his dreams, of fresh dates, a miswak, migrating to Yathrib, a broken sword and cows, and two gold bangles he took as two liars, one Musailima.
Allah chose Kinana from Ishmael's descendants, then Quraysh, Banu Hashim and the Prophet; a stone in Mecca greeted him before prophethood, and he will be first intercessor on Resurrection Day.
Water spouted from the Prophet's fingers for many to make ablution, and Umm Malik's butter skin and a man's barley kept providing until she squeezed it and he weighed it.
On the Tabuk expedition the Prophet combined prayers, a trickling spring gushed for all, a storm he foretold struck, and returning he praised Uhud and ranked the Ansar's houses.
In Najd a man seized the sleeping Prophet's sword and asked who could protect him; he answered 'Allah', the man sheathed it, and the Prophet did not touch him.
The Prophet likened his guidance to rain on three kinds of land, himself to a man warning of an army, and his people to moths he holds back from fire.
The Prophet likened himself among the earlier Apostles to the one missing brick in a fine house, the last of the Apostles who completes the building.
When Allah wills mercy for a community He takes its Apostle as a forerunner, and when He wills its destruction He destroys it in its Apostle's lifetime for belying him.
The Prophet will precede his people at the Cistern, whose drinkers never thirst, but some he knows will be kept from him, he being told they turned back after him.
After praying over Uhud's martyrs, the Prophet told the people from the pulpit he would precede them at the Cistern, fearing for them not polytheism but vying for worldly treasures.
At the Cistern the Prophet will plead for some people as his companions but must yield, being told he does not know what innovations they made after him.
The Cistern spans the distance between San'a and Medina, Jarba and Adhruh, or Amman and Aila; its vessels outnumber the stars, and its water, fed from Paradise, ends all thirst.
The Prophet will push crowds back from his Cistern and drive some away like stray camels; its water is whiter than milk and sweeter than honey, fed from Paradise.
At Uhud Sa'd saw two men in white, Gabriel and Michael, fighting fiercely at the Prophet's right and left, never seen by him before or after.
The Prophet was the best, most generous and bravest of people, riding ahead to check an alarm in Medina, and most generous of all in Ramadan when Gabriel met him.
Anas served the Prophet for nine or ten years at home and travelling, and he never spoke harshly to him or asked why he had done or left anything.
The Prophet never refused a request; he gave one man a huge flock and Safwan three hundred camels, and after his death Abu Bakr paid Jabir what he had promised.
The Prophet, kindest of all to his family, wept as his infant son Ibrahim died, saying only what pleases Allah, and said two foster-mothers would complete his suckling in Paradise.
The Prophet kissed children, including Hasan; to those who never kissed theirs he spoke of Allah depriving hearts of mercy, and said whoever shows no mercy is shown none.
The Prophet was more modest than a secluded virgin, never coarse or reviling, called the best those best in morals, and only smiled when his Companions laughed.
The Prophet told Anjasha, the melodious camel-driver leading his wives' mounts, to drive slowly, for he was carrying vessels of glass, meaning the weak women.
After dawn prayer the Prophet dipped his hand in every water vessel Medina's servants brought, even on cold mornings, and his Companions sought to catch every hair the barber cut.
The Prophet stood aside until a deranged woman's need was met, chose the easier course unless sinful, struck no woman or servant, and avenged only violations of Allah's limits.
The Prophet's hand and body were more fragrant than musk and softer than silk, and Umm Sulaim collected his sweat as perfume and for blessing her children.
Revelation came to the Prophet like a ringing bell or through an angel in human form, weighing on him, changing his colour, bowing his head and making his forehead sweat.
The Prophet let his hair fall like the People of the Book, later parting it; he was of medium height, broad-shouldered and handsome, with hair to his ears or shoulders.
Anas said the Prophet did not dye his few white hairs, mostly at chin and temples, though Abu Bakr and Umar used henna; Abu Juhaifa and Jabir described them too.
Jabir b. Samura, As-Sa'ib b. Yazid and Abdullah b. Sarjis saw the seal of prophethood between the Prophet's shoulders, the size of a pigeon's egg, and Jabir described his face.
Reports give the Prophet's commission at forty, his age at death as sixty or sixty-three, like Abu Bakr and Umar, and his stay in Mecca as ten or thirteen years.
